headline: Young Hacker Admits Guilt After Leaking Secret Video Game Footage

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: A few years ago, someone broke into a video game company's computers without permission. This is called hacking. The hacker stole secret videos from a game called Grand Theft Auto VI before it was even finished, and shared them online. This made the game company very upset because the videos were supposed to be a surprise. The hacker's name is Arion Kurtaj, and he was part of a group of hackers. He also broke into phone companies and other big businesses. Because he was young and had autism, which means his brain works a little differently than most people's, the court first sent him to a special hospital instead of jail. Later, doctors said he was ready to go to a regular court. This week, Kurtaj said he was guilty of these computer crimes. He will find out his punishment on November 23rd. That is just a few days after the real Grand Theft Auto VI game finally comes out for everyone to play. This story shows why it's so important to keep computer passwords and information safe and private.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: In 2022, a hacker leaked 90 secret videos from the unfinished video game Grand Theft Auto VI. The person responsible, Arion Kurtaj, was part of a hacking group called Lapsus$. Hackers are people who break into computer systems without permission, often to steal private information. Kurtaj didn't just target the game company, Rockstar Games. He also hacked a phone company, Uber, and a banking app called Revolut. One of his tricks was something called a 'SIM swap,' where a hacker tricks a phone company into moving someone's phone number to a new device, which lets them steal texts, calls, and even security codes. Kurtaj was first arrested for hacking the phone company. While waiting for his case, he was moved to a hotel for safety, but he broke the rules by using a phone, a hotel TV's internet connection, and a streaming device to keep hacking companies. Because Kurtaj has autism, a condition that affects how someone thinks, communicates, or behaves, a court first sent him to a secure hospital instead of prison. Later, he was found ready to stand trial and was moved to prison. This week, Kurtaj admitted he was guilty of the hacking crimes. He will learn his punishment on November 23rd, just four days after Grand Theft Auto VI is finally released to the public. This case reminds us how valuable and vulnerable people's private data and companies' secrets can be, and how seriously the law treats stealing them.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: A young hacker named Arion Kurtaj has admitted he committed a string of major cybercrimes, including the theft and leak of 90 unreleased videos from the highly anticipated game Grand Theft Auto VI in 2022. Kurtaj was a member of Lapsus$, a hacking group known for breaking into large companies and stealing confidential information, sometimes to prove they could, and sometimes to demand money or attention. Before the GTA VI leak, Kurtaj had already hacked the phone company BT/EE sometime in 2021, using a method called 'SIM swapping.' This involves tricking a phone carrier into transferring someone's phone number to a device controlled by the hacker, allowing them to intercept calls, texts, and security codes meant for the real owner. After being charged for that crime, Kurtaj was placed in a hotel for his own protection while his case was pending. However, he broke the rules of his release by continuing to hack major companies, including Rockstar Games (the maker of GTA VI), Uber, and the financial app Revolut, using nothing more than a phone, the hotel's Wi-Fi, and a small streaming device called a Firestick. Because Kurtaj has autism, a condition that can affect communication, thinking, and behavior, a court initially ruled he should be sent to a secure hospital rather than prison. However, earlier this year, doctors determined he was mentally fit to stand trial, so he was transferred to prison instead. This week, Kurtaj pleaded guilty to the hacking-related charges against him. His sentencing is scheduled for November 23rd, just days after GTA VI is officially released to players around the world. This case highlights how even unfinished, unreleased creative work can be extremely valuable and vulnerable to theft, and how companies must constantly guard against breaches not just of money, but of ideas, plans, and products still in development. It also raises interesting questions about how the justice system handles crimes committed by people with disabilities, and how much responsibility someone should bear for actions taken even after being caught once.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: Arion Kurtaj, a 21-year-old member of the hacking collective Lapsus$, has pleaded guilty to a series of cybercrimes that included leaking 90 unreleased development videos from Grand Theft Auto VI in 2022, one of the most anticipated video games ever made. Lapsus$ became notorious for breaching major corporations, often publicizing stolen data to embarrass companies or demonstrate the group's capabilities rather than purely for financial gain. Kurtaj's criminal activity began earlier, when he hacked the telecommunications company BT/EE sometime between August and November 2021. His method involved 'SIM swapping,' a technique where a hacker convinces a phone carrier to transfer someone's phone number onto a device the hacker controls. Once completed, this allows the attacker to intercept calls, text messages, and security verification codes meant for the real account holder, effectively letting them bypass many security protections tied to a phone number. After BT/EE noticed a surge in unauthorized SIM swaps, investigators traced the activity back to Kurtaj, leading to charges. While awaiting trial, he was placed in a hotel under supervision for his own protection, but he violated the conditions of his release by continuing to hack companies using only a mobile phone, the hotel television's Wi-Fi connection, and a Firestick streaming device. During this period, he targeted Rockstar Games, Uber, and the financial technology company Revolut. Because Kurtaj has autism, which can affect how a person processes information, communicates, and manages impulses, a court initially ordered him to be held in a secure hospital rather than a standard prison following his conviction in December 2023. However, this past January, medical professionals determined that he was fit to stand trial, resulting in his transfer to a conventional prison facility. His guilty plea this week resolves the legal proceedings tied to these hacking incidents, and he is scheduled to be formally sentenced on November 23rd, just four days after Grand Theft Auto VI's actual public release on November 19th. This case illustrates several important realities about modern technology: that creative and corporate work-in-progress can be just as valuable a target for theft as finished products or financial data, that everyday communication tools like phone numbers can be exploited as security weaknesses, and that the justice system must carefully balance punishment with considerations like mental health and neurodivergence when determining appropriate consequences for a crime.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: Arion Kurtaj, now 21 and a former member of the cybercrime group Lapsus$, has pleaded guilty to a series of high-profile hacking offenses, most notably the 2022 leak of 90 unreleased development videos from Grand Theft Auto VI, one of the gaming industry's most eagerly awaited titles. Lapsus$ gained international attention for breaching the security systems of numerous large corporations, often releasing stolen internal data publicly rather than seeking ransom, which distinguished the group from more traditional financially motivated cybercriminal organizations. Kurtaj's documented offenses began with an attack on the telecommunications company BT/EE sometime between August and November 2021. His primary technique was SIM swapping, a form of identity-based fraud in which an attacker persuades or manipulates a phone carrier into transferring a victim's phone number to a SIM card controlled by the attacker. Because many modern security systems rely on text-message verification codes sent to a person's phone, gaining control of that number can allow a hacker to bypass two-factor authentication and access emails, bank accounts, and other sensitive services. BT/EE detected a sharp rise in unauthorized SIM swaps beginning in November 2021, which ultimately led investigators to Kurtaj and resulted in formal charges against him. While his case was pending, authorities relocated Kurtaj to a hotel, reportedly for his own safety given the attention surrounding his case. Despite this arrangement, he violated the terms of his bail by continuing his hacking activities from within the hotel, relying only on a mobile phone, the hotel television's Wi-Fi network, and a small streaming device known as a Firestick. During this period he carried out additional breaches against Rockstar Games, the ride-sharing company Uber, and the financial technology firm Revolut, demonstrating that even restricted access to basic internet-connected devices can be enough to carry out sophisticated cyberattacks. Kurtaj's legal proceedings have also drawn attention to how the justice system addresses neurodivergence in criminal cases. Because he has autism, a developmental condition that can influence communication, social understanding, and behavioral regulation, a court in December 2023 initially ordered that he be held in a secure psychiatric hospital rather than a conventional prison, despite having already been found responsible for his actions. This arrangement was revisited in January, when medical evaluators determined that Kurtaj was fit to stand trial, prompting his transfer to prison. His guilty plea this week effectively closes the central criminal proceedings connected to these incidents, with formal sentencing scheduled for November 23rd, just days after Grand Theft Auto VI's long-awaited public release on November 19th. Beyond the individual case, the episode underscores broader concerns in cybersecurity: that unfinished creative and technical work can be just as valuable a target as finished products or financial assets, that identity verification systems built around phone numbers remain a significant vulnerability, and that the legal system continues to grapple with how best to balance accountability, public safety, and fair treatment for offenders whose cognitive or developmental differences complicate traditional notions of culpability and detention.

questions: If someone shared secret or unfinished work you created online without your permission, how do you think that would affect you, and what should happen to the person who did it?

This story shows how phone numbers can be used to break into accounts through 'SIM swapping' — what steps do you think people, schools, or companies should take to protect personal information online?

The court had to decide how to handle punishment for someone with autism who broke the law. Why might it be important, or difficult, for courts to consider a person's personal circumstances when deciding consequences?
